Context: This reference book was written for the U.S. government in the 1980s; the passage describes the spring of 1968 in Czechoslovakia.

"In April the KSC Presidium adopted the Action Program that had been drafted by a coalition headed by Dubcek and made up of reformers, moderates, centrists, and conservatives. The program proposed a "new model of socialism," profoundly "democratic" and "national," that is, adapted to Czechoslovak conditions. The National Front and the electoral system were to be democratized, and Czechoslovakia was to be federalized. Freedom of assembly and expression would be guaranteed in constitutional law. The New Economic Model was to be implemented. The Action Program also reaffirmed the Czechoslovak alliance with the Soviet Union and other socialist states. The reform movement, which rejected Stalinism as the road to communism, remained committed to communism as a goal. The Action Program stipulated that reform must proceed under KSC direction."

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE way the excerpt indicates that the reformers of 1968 meant to keep their changes within the limits of communist rule.
parts.model_answer: The excerpt says the Action Program reaffirmed Czechoslovakia's alliance with the Soviet Union and other socialist states, which shows the reformers did not plan to leave the Soviet bloc.

rubric_rows.criterion: The response describes a feature of the excerpt that shows the reforms were meant to stay inside communist rule, for example that the program reaffirmed the alliance with the Soviet Union and other socialist states, kept communism as the goal while rejecting only Stalinism, or required that reform go forward under KSC direction.
required_elements: The excerpt says the Action Program reaffirmed Czechoslovakia's alliance with the Soviet Union and other socialist states, which shows the reformers did not plan to leave the Soviet bloc.
The excerpt says the reform movement rejected Stalinism but remained committed to communism as a goal, so it aimed to change methods rather than abandon communism.
The excerpt says the Action Program stipulated that reform must proceed under KSC direction, so the Communist Party would keep control of the process.
The excerpt calls the program a new model of socialism, which presents the changes as a version of socialism adapted to Czechoslovak conditions rather than a break with it.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific historical development in Czechoslovakia or the Soviet bloc between 1956 and August 1968 that helps explain why reformers in Czechoslovakia pursued changes like those described in the excerpt. Do not use the Action Program or the New Economic Model themselves as your answer.
parts.model_answer: De-Stalinization after Khrushchev's 1956 speech criticizing Stalin weakened the authority of hard-line leaders and encouraged communists in Czechoslovakia to imagine a less repressive socialism.

rubric_rows.criterion: The response explains a specific development from 1956 to August 1968 that helps explain the push for reform, such as de-Stalinization after Khrushchev's 1956 speech, economic slowdown in Czechoslovakia in the early 1960s, the replacement of Antonin Novotny by Alexander Dubcek in January 1968, Slovak resentment of centralized rule, or the lifting of press censorship and the growth of public debate in spring 1968.
required_elements: De-Stalinization after Khrushchev's 1956 speech criticizing Stalin weakened the authority of hard-line leaders and encouraged communists in Czechoslovakia to imagine a less repressive socialism.
Slow economic growth in Czechoslovakia in the early 1960s discredited rigid central planning and led economists such as Ota Sik to argue for market-based reforms.
In January 1968 reform-minded party members replaced Antonin Novotny with Alexander Dubcek as First Secretary, giving reformers control of party leadership.
Many Slovaks resented centralized rule from Prague, and that pressure helps explain why the reform program called for federalizing the country.
When censorship was lifted in spring 1968, open discussion in the press and new citizens' clubs spread public demands for wider freedoms.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific effect of the Soviet-led military intervention in Czechoslovakia in August 1968, either within Czechoslovakia or elsewhere in Europe, in the period 1968-1989.
parts.model_answer: The intervention led to the Brezhnev Doctrine, which claimed a right for the Soviet bloc to intervene in any socialist state where socialism seemed threatened and shaped bloc politics until the late 1980s.

rubric_rows.criterion: The response explains a specific effect of the August 1968 intervention between 1968 and 1989, such as the Brezhnev Doctrine, Dubcek's removal and Husak's normalization, purges and renewed censorship, protests such as Jan Palach's self-immolation in January 1969, criticism from Romania or Western communist parties, or later dissent such as Charter 77.
required_elements: The intervention led to the Brezhnev Doctrine, which claimed a right for the Soviet bloc to intervene in any socialist state where socialism seemed threatened and shaped bloc politics until the late 1980s.
Dubcek was removed in April 1969 and replaced by Gustav Husak, whose normalization brought purges of reformers from the party, renewed censorship and an end to most of the Prague Spring reforms.
Jan Palach set himself on fire in January 1969 to protest the occupation, which made him a lasting symbol of resistance in Czechoslovakia.
Romania condemned the invasion and Western communist parties such as the Italian Communist Party criticized it, deepening divisions in European communism.
The failure of reform from within the party led later dissidents such as the authors of Charter 77 in 1977 to frame opposition in terms of human rights rather than reforming the party.

Sample response, high score (3/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 1):
(A) The excerpt shows the reformers wanted to stay inside communist rule because the Action Program "stipulated that reform must proceed under KSC direction." So even with new freedoms like assembly and expression, the Communist Party would stay in charge and no other party would take power. The program also reaffirmed the alliance with the Soviet Union, which was meant to show Moscow that Czechoslovakia was not going to leave the bloc the way Hungary tried to in 1956.

(B) One development that explains the reforms is the economic slowdown in Czechoslovakia in the early 1960s, when growth fell badly and the third Five-Year Plan had to be abandoned. This made it clear that Stalinist central planning was failing, so economists like Ota Sik and other reformers in the party argued for market elements and more open debate. It also led to the replacement of Antonin Novotny by Alexander Dubcek as party leader in January 1968, which gave the reformers the power to put changes like the ones in the excerpt into action.

(C) One effect of the intervention was the Brezhnev Doctrine, which said the Soviet bloc had the right to intervene in any socialist country where socialism was threatened. Inside Czechoslovakia, Dubcek was removed in April 1969 and replaced by Gustav Husak, who led "normalization," purging reformers from the party and bringing back censorship. This repression led to later dissent, like Charter 77 in 1977, where people like Vaclav Havel criticized the government for not respecting human rights.

   - "purging reformers from the party and bringing back censorship" - Accurate detail on Husak's normalization within Czechoslovakia, which strengthens the explained effect.

(A) One way the excerpt shows the reformers wanted to stay inside communist rule is that the Action Program said reform had to go forward under KSC direction. This means the Communist Party would still be in charge and the reformers were not trying to end one-party rule or bring back capitalism. The excerpt also says the program reaffirmed the alliance with the Soviet Union and other socialist states, so they were not trying to leave the Soviet bloc.

(B) A development before 1968 that led to reform was the time after Stalin died when things in the Soviet bloc were changing. facts: Alexander Dubcek replaced Antonin Novotny as First Secretary of the Czechoslovak Communist Party in January 1968.
The KSC Presidium adopted the Action Program in April 1968.
Press censorship was relaxed and then lifted during spring 1968, and open public debate grew.
The Two Thousand Words manifesto, written by Ludvik Vaculik, was published in June 1968 and called for faster reform.
On the night of 20-21 August 1968, troops from the Soviet Union and several Warsaw Pact allies invaded Czechoslovakia.
Romania refused to take part in the intervention, and its leader Nicolae Ceausescu condemned it publicly.
Czechoslovak leaders were taken to Moscow and signed the Moscow Protocol in August 1968, which committed them to roll back reforms.
The Brezhnev Doctrine, stated in autumn 1968, claimed the right of socialist states to intervene when socialism was threatened in another socialist state.
The student Jan Palach set himself on fire in Prague in January 1969 to protest the occupation and the loss of reforms.
Gustav Husak replaced Dubcek as party leader in April 1969 and led the policy known as normalization.
Federalization took effect on 1 January 1969, creating Czech and Slovak socialist republics within Czechoslovakia.
Charter 77, a human rights declaration whose spokesmen included Vaclav Havel, appeared in January 1977.
Khrushchev's 1956 speech criticizing Stalin started de-Stalinization across the Soviet bloc.

parts.prompt:
Between the Three Emperors' League of 1881 and the Locarno agreements of 1925, European governments signed many treaties, conventions and alliances. Some promised to localize conflicts or guarantee frontiers. Others committed armies to mobilize, divided regions into spheres of influence, or assigned responsibility for a war. The seven documents include treaty texts signed by the great powers, a painting of the 1919 signing at Versailles by a British official war artist, and the memoirs of the former German emperor.

Evaluate the extent to which diplomatic agreements among European powers between 1881 and 1925 were aimed at preserving peace and security rather than at advancing the interests of individual states.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
- Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
- Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
- For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
- Demonstrate a complex understanding of the historical development that is the focus of the prompt, using evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the question.
parts.model_answer:
Between 1881 and 1925 European diplomats often used the language of peace, but most agreements before 1914 were really about protecting individual states against specific rivals, and they ended up dividing Europe into armed blocs. After the destruction of the First World War the purpose shifted somewhat. Versailles was still shaped by the winners' interests, but Locarno was a more genuine attempt at collective security, although even it served the national interests of France and Germany.

The background to these agreements is the change in the balance of power after German unification in 1871. A new, powerful Germany in the center of Europe worried its neighbors, and France wanted revenge for losing Alsace-Lorraine. Bismarck tried to keep France isolated by tying the other great powers to Germany. At the same time, the New Imperialism made the powers compete for colonies and influence in Africa and Asia, so diplomacy was not only about European borders but also about empire. This competition explains why so many treaties talked about "interests."

The Three Emperors' League of 1881 (Doc 1) seems peaceful at first, because it promises "benevolent neutrality" and the "localization of the conflict." But the treaty was secret, which shows it was not meant to reassure Europe as a whole. Its real purpose for Germany was to keep Russia and Austria-Hungary from fighting each other in the Balkans and to keep France without allies. The clause about taking "account of their respective interests in the Balkan Peninsula" shows that the main concern was the interests of the three empires. Bismarck kept this up with the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1887, but when it was allowed to lapse in 1890, Russia was left free to look for a new partner.

That partner was France. The Franco-Russian Military Convention of 1892 (Doc 2) is defensive in wording, since it only applies "if France is attacked by Germany." However, it was written by the French and Russian general staffs, so it reflects military thinking more than diplomatic thinking. Military officers were focused on winning a war, not preventing one, which is why the treaty says both countries will mobilize "immediately and simultaneously" as soon as any Triple Alliance power mobilizes. This made a local crisis much more likely to turn into a general war, which is what happened in 1914.

The Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 (Doc 3) complicates the picture. By drawing a line across Persia that Britain would not cross for concessions, it reduced the old imperial rivalry between Britain and Russia, so in a way it did preserve peace between those two. But it did this by dividing up another country's economy for their own benefit, and it also helped bring Britain closer to the France and Russia bloc. So peace and self-interest overlapped here instead of being opposites.

After the war, the Treaty of Versailles (Doc 4) assigned "the responsibility of Germany and her allies" for the war in Article 231. The winners claimed this was about justice and security, but it also served their interest in getting reparations, even though Article 232 admits Germany's resources were "not adequate" to pay everything. Orpen's painting (Doc 5) shows the signing in the Hall of Mirrors, the same place where the German Empire was proclaimed in 1871, under gilded decoration and the inscription "Le roy gouverne." As a British official war artist, Orpen was presenting the victors' ceremony, and the setting itself was a message of French triumph over Germany. Wilhelm II's memoirs (Doc 6) show the German side of this resentment. Writing in exile after abdicating, he had a reason to blame England's jealousy of German "peaceful penetration" of markets instead of German policy, so his account is self-serving, but it does show how national economic rivalry was behind prewar tensions.

Locarno in 1925 (Doc 7) is different because it was public and included defeated Germany as an equal partner. Germany and France promised they would "in no case attack or invade each other," and the powers "collectively" guaranteed the borders. Still, it only guaranteed Germany's western frontiers, not the eastern ones, which suited Germany's interests.

Overall, the agreements from 1881 to 1914 mainly advanced state interests under defensive language, while the postwar agreements moved, unevenly, toward real collective security.

Examples: alliances that were defensive in wording served each state's security against particular rivals; or there was a shift from bloc-building before 1914 to collective guarantees at Locarno.

Places the agreements in a broader setting, such as the European balance of power after German unification in 1871 and the Congress of Berlin, the imperial competition of the New Imperialism, the arms race and growing alliance blocs, or the destruction of the First World War and the instability of the early 1920s.

Uses what the documents actually say: the localization and Balkan clauses of the 1881 treaty, the mobilization commitments of 1892, the line dividing concessions in Persia, Articles 231 and 232, the Versailles setting in Orpen's painting, Wilhelm II's account of German economic rise, and the Locarno frontier guarantee and non-aggression pledge.

Gives at least one accurate, specific piece of evidence that is not in the documents and uses it in the argument. Examples: the Dual Alliance of 1879, the Triple Alliance of 1882, the Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 and its lapse in 1890, the Entente Cordiale of 1904, the Moroccan crises, the Bosnian crisis of 1908, the League of Nations, the Ruhr occupation of 1923, the Dawes Plan of 1924.

Examples: the treaties of 1881 and 1892 were secret, the 1892 convention was drafted by general staffs, Orpen was a British official war artist, Wilhelm II wrote in exile after abdicating, and Locarno was a public agreement that included defeated Germany.

Shows a complex understanding. Examples: treating peace and state interest as overlapping rather than opposite, since defensive alliances and spheres of influence lowered some tensions and sharpened others; explaining change over time from secret bloc treaties to public collective guarantees; or corroborating and qualifying claims across several documents and sources.

Scoring guide (ALTON reference — not official AP scoring). This question is worth 7 points.
Thesis/claim (0-1): The thesis has to take a position on how far the agreements from 1881 to 1925 aimed at peace and security versus the interests of individual states, and it has to give a reason that organizes the essay. Examples: alliances that were defensive in wording served each state's security against particular rivals; or there was a shift from bloc-building before 1914 to collective guarantees at Locarno.
   - 1: Makes a defensible claim about the extent to which the agreements aimed at peace and security rather than state interests, with a line of reasoning, in the introduction or conclusion.
   - 0: Gives no defensible claim, only restates the prompt, or does not weigh peace and security against state interests.
Contextualization (0-1): Places the agreements in a broader setting, such as the European balance of power after German unification in 1871 and the Congress of Berlin, the imperial competition of the New Imperialism, the arms race and growing alliance blocs, or the destruction of the First World War and the instability of the early 1920s.
   - 1: Describes a broader development before, during or after 1881 to 1925 and connects it to the argument about the purposes of the agreements.
   - 0: Gives no relevant context, or only mentions a phrase or date without explaining it.
Evidence from the documents (0-2): Uses what the documents actually say: the localization and Balkan clauses of the 1881 treaty, the mobilization commitments of 1892, the line dividing concessions in Persia, Articles 231 and 232, the Versailles setting in Orpen's painting, Wilhelm II's account of German economic rise, and the Locarno frontier guarantee and non-aggression pledge.
   - 2: Uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument about the extent to which the agreements aimed at peace and security rather than state interests.
   - 1: Accurately describes the content of at least three documents and relates them to the topic.
   - 0: Uses fewer than three documents accurately, or only quotes them without connecting them to the topic.

Examples: the Dual Alliance of 1879, the Triple Alliance of 1882, the Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 and its lapse in 1890, the Entente Cordiale of 1904, the Moroccan crises, the Bosnian crisis of 1908, the League of Nations, the Ruhr occupation of 1923, the Dawes Plan of 1924.
   - 1: Uses at least one specific, accurate piece of outside evidence to support an argument about the purposes of the agreements.
   - 0: Gives no outside evidence, or the evidence is inaccurate or merely named.

Examples: the treaties of 1881 and 1892 were secret, the 1892 convention was drafted by general staffs, Orpen was a British official war artist, Wilhelm II wrote in exile after abdicating, and Locarno was a public agreement that included defeated Germany.
   - 1: For at least two documents, explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience matters to the argument.

   - 1: Shows complex understanding through sustained analysis, such as weighing multiple causes or purposes, explaining change and continuity, or using the documents to qualify the argument.
   - 0: Gives no complex understanding, or only mentions complexity in a phrase.

Do not require students to identify individual delegates.

Evidence map (which documents support or complicate each line of reasoning):
- Agreements aimed at preserving peace by localizing conflicts and guaranteeing frontiers. Supports: Document 1, 7. Complicates: Document 2, 4.
- Agreements mainly advanced the strategic, imperial or economic interests of individual states. Supports: Document 2, 3, 4, 6. Complicates: Document 7.
- Defensive security for some states produced rival blocs and insecurity for others. Supports: Document 1, 2, 6. Complicates: Document 3.
- The postwar settlement moved from a victors' peace toward mutual guarantees. Supports: Document 4, 5, 7. Complicates: Document 6.

Using the documents (use and sourcing):
- Document 1: Peace aims: benevolent neutrality and efforts toward the 'localization of the conflict', plus a pledge to avoid 'discord' in the Balkans. State interest: it protects Austria-Hungary's position under the Treaty of Berlin and each court's 'respective interests'. Sourcing: It was a secret treaty among three monarchies, so it was meant for the governments themselves, not the public. It shows the powers managing their own Balkan rivalry while promising neutrality only to each other, not to Europe as a whole.
- Document 2: State interest and the forming of blocs: France and Russia each pledge 'all her available forces' against Germany and promise immediate mobilization if the Triple Alliance mobilizes. This can be read as defensive security or as preparation for war. Sourcing: Army officers of the two general staffs signed it in secret. Its purpose was military planning, which explains its focus on mobilization and moving troops to the frontiers rather than on settling disputes.
- Document 3: State interest through imperial spheres: Britain agrees not to seek railway, bank or other concessions beyond a fixed line and not to oppose Russian-backed concessions there. - Document 4: State interest and victors' security: Article 231 has Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage of a war 'imposed' by German aggression. - Document 5: The Versailles settlement as a ceremony of victory: the signing takes place in the gilded Hall of Mirrors under an inscription beginning 'Le roy gouverne', and the delegates are small beneath the grand architecture. It can be used for the idea of a peace imposed with symbols of power. Sourcing: Orpen was a British official war artist, so his view comes from the victors' side. The setting itself matters: the Hall of Mirrors was where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871.

It can also be read as confirming the Versailles settlement in the interest of France and Belgium. Sourcing: Unlike the secret treaties of 1881 and 1892, this agreement included defeated Germany as an equal party. The situation after the Ruhr crisis matters. It covers only the frontiers of Germany with France and Belgium.

defensible_theses: Most agreements from 1881 to 1914 were written in the language of peace, but each one mainly served a signatory's security against particular rivals or its imperial ambitions. The 1881 promise to localize conflicts, the 1892 mobilization pledge and the 1907 division of Persia protected individual states and hardened rival blocs. After the war, the Versailles settlement imposed the victors' interests, and Locarno in 1925 was a limited move toward collective guarantees.

The aims of these agreements changed over time. Bismarck's alliances of the 1880s tried to keep the peace by isolating France and managing Austro-Russian rivalry in the Balkans. The military and imperial agreements of the 1890s and 1900s put national advantage and readiness for war first. The Locarno Pact turned back toward mutual security by having former enemies guarantee frontiers together.

Peace and state interest were not opposites, because great powers thought their own security was the same thing as peace. Each agreement promoted peace for some states by preparing for war or imposing terms on others. That is why the 1892 convention, Article 231 and even Locarno, which guaranteed only Germany's western borders, lowered some tensions and created others.
contextualization_ideas: After German unification in 1871 and the proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles, Bismarck tried to isolate France and keep Austria-Hungary and Russia from fighting over the Balkans. The Congress of Berlin in 1878 had left Austro-Russian rivalry there unresolved.

The New Imperialism of the late nineteenth century, including the Scramble for Africa and competition in Central Asia (the Great Game between Britain and Russia), made great-power agreements partly about colonial spheres and markets.

The First World War caused enormous loss of life, the collapse of the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires, and economic disruption. This shaped the Paris Peace Conference, the founding of the League of Nations, and the crises of the early 1920s such as the Ruhr occupation.
outside_evidence: The Dual Alliance of 1879 between Germany and Austria-Hungary, and the Triple Alliance of 1882, which added Italy.
The Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 between Germany and Russia, which Germany did not renew in 1890 after Bismarck's dismissal. This opened the way for Franco-Russian cooperation.
The Entente Cordiale of 1904 between Britain and France settled colonial disputes, including recognition of British interests in Egypt and French interests in Morocco.
The First Moroccan Crisis and the Algeciras Conference of 1906, and the Second Moroccan Crisis of 1911, tested the alliance blocs.
The Bosnian annexation crisis of 1908, when Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina, angered Serbia and Russia.
The Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 set rules for European claims in Africa.
Wilson's Fourteen Points and the Covenant of the League of Nations proposed collective security after the war.
The French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr in 1923 and the Dawes Plan of 1924, which rescheduled German reparation payments.
Germany entered the League of Nations in 1926 after Locarno. Briand and Stresemann received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926.

samples.essay:
Between 1881 and 1925 European diplomats often used the language of peace, but most agreements before 1914 were really about protecting individual states against specific rivals, and they ended up dividing Europe into armed blocs. After the destruction of the First World War the purpose shifted somewhat. Versailles was still shaped by the winners' interests, but Locarno was a more genuine attempt at collective security, although even it served the national interests of France and Germany.

The background to these agreements is the change in the balance of power after German unification in 1871. A new, powerful Germany in the center of Europe worried its neighbors, and France wanted revenge for losing Alsace-Lorraine. Bismarck tried to keep France isolated by tying the other great powers to Germany. At the same time, the New Imperialism made the powers compete for colonies and influence in Africa and Asia, so diplomacy was not only about European borders but also about empire. This competition explains why so many treaties talked about "interests."

The Three Emperors' League of 1881 (Doc 1) seems peaceful at first, because it promises "benevolent neutrality" and the "localization of the conflict." But the treaty was secret, which shows it was not meant to reassure Europe as a whole. Its real purpose for Germany was to keep Russia and Austria-Hungary from fighting each other in the Balkans and to keep France without allies. The clause about taking "account of their respective interests in the Balkan Peninsula" shows that the main concern was the interests of the three empires. Bismarck kept this up with the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1887, but when it was allowed to lapse in 1890, Russia was left free to look for a new partner.

That partner was France. The Franco-Russian Military Convention of 1892 (Doc 2) is defensive in wording, since it only applies "if France is attacked by Germany." However, it was written by the French and Russian general staffs, so it reflects military thinking more than diplomatic thinking. Military officers were focused on winning a war, not preventing one, which is why the treaty says both countries will mobilize "immediately and simultaneously" as soon as any Triple Alliance power mobilizes. This made a local crisis much more likely to turn into a general war, which is what happened in 1914.

The Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 (Doc 3) complicates the picture. By drawing a line across Persia that Britain would not cross for concessions, it reduced the old imperial rivalry between Britain and Russia, so in a way it did preserve peace between those two. But it did this by dividing up another country's economy for their own benefit, and it also helped bring Britain closer to the France and Russia bloc. So peace and self-interest overlapped here instead of being opposites.

After the war, the Treaty of Versailles (Doc 4) assigned "the responsibility of Germany and her allies" for the war in Article 231. The winners claimed this was about justice and security, but it also served their interest in getting reparations, even though Article 232 admits Germany's resources were "not adequate" to pay everything. Orpen's painting (Doc 5) shows the signing in the Hall of Mirrors, the same place where the German Empire was proclaimed in 1871, under gilded decoration and the inscription "Le roy gouverne." As a British official war artist, Orpen was presenting the victors' ceremony, and the setting itself was a message of French triumph over Germany. Wilhelm II's memoirs (Doc 6) show the German side of this resentment. Writing in exile after abdicating, he had a reason to blame England's jealousy of German "peaceful penetration" of markets instead of German policy, so his account is self-serving, but it does show how national economic rivalry was behind prewar tensions.

Locarno in 1925 (Doc 7) is different because it was public and included defeated Germany as an equal partner. Germany and France promised they would "in no case attack or invade each other," and the powers "collectively" guaranteed the borders. Still, it only guaranteed Germany's western frontiers, not the eastern ones, which suited Germany's interests.

Overall, the agreements from 1881 to 1914 mainly advanced state interests under defensive language, while the postwar agreements moved, unevenly, toward real collective security.

Context: Christopher Columbus was an Italian-born navigator sailing for the Spanish crown; he wrote this letter in 1493 on the voyage home from his first voyage across the Atlantic.

"Española is a wonder. Its mountains and plains, and meadows, and fields, are so beautiful and rich for planting and sowing, and rearing cattle of all kinds, and for building towns and villages. The harbours on the coast, and the number and size and wholesomeness of the rivers, most of them bearing gold, surpass anything that would be believed by one who had not seen them. [...] Although I have taken possession of all these islands in the name of their Highnesses, and they are all more abundant in wealth than I am able to express; and although I hold them all for their Highnesses, so that they can dispose of them quite as absolutely as they can of the kingdoms of Castile, yet there was one large town in Española of which especially I took possession, situated in a locality well adapted for the working of the gold mines, and for all kinds of commerce, either with the main land on this side, or with that beyond which is the land of the great Khan, with which there will be vast commerce and great profit."

parts.model_answer: Columbus claims that Española's mountains, plains and fields are rich enough for planting crops, raising cattle and building towns, which presents the island as good land for settlement.

Columbus states that he has taken possession of the islands for Ferdinand and Isabella and that they can control them as completely as they control the kingdom of Castile.

This success showed Castile that sea voyages could bring in gold and trade, which explains why Columbus stresses gold and commerce.

rubric_rows.criterion: The response explains a specific Portuguese or Spanish development from 1450 to 1500 and connects it to Columbus's goals of gold, trade with Asia or claiming land for the crown. Good examples are Portuguese voyages along the African coast and the gold trade at Elmina, Dias rounding the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, the agreement Ferdinand and Isabella made with Columbus in 1492 after the conquest of Granada, or the race with Portugal that led to the Treaty of Tordesillas.
required_elements: During the fifteenth century Portuguese voyages backed by Prince Henry and later kings worked their way down the West African coast, and Portugal's fort at Elmina (built 1482) gave it access to African gold. In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope, which opened an eastern sea route toward Asia for Portugal. Spain was competing for its own route to Asian trade, which explains why Columbus points to future commerce with the land of the great Khan.

parts.prompt:
Between the publication of Rousseau's Emile in 1762 and the outbreak of the First World War in 1914, European writers argued about women's nature, education, and rights, and by the late nineteenth century organized movements were campaigning for women's political rights, above all the parliamentary vote. Laws on marriage, property, education, and the franchise changed in some places and stayed fixed in others.

Evaluate the extent to which ideas and political movements changed the legal and social position of women in Europe between 1762 and 1914.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
- Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
- Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
- For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
- Use evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the prompt.
parts.model_answer:
Between 1762 and 1914, ideas about women's equality changed a great deal, but the legal position of women changed much less. Writers like Wollstonecraft and Mill attacked the idea that women were naturally meant to obey men, and by the late 1800s these arguments had turned into organized mass movements. However, the movements were divided over methods, and by 1914 most European women still could not vote in national elections, so the change was mostly in ideas and organization and only partly in law.

The debate over women took place in a wider context of Enlightenment arguments about natural rights and reason. Thinkers argued that all men had rights by nature, and the French Revolution put these ideas into practice for men, but not for women. Later, industrialization helped spread the ideology of separate spheres, where middle class men worked in public and women were supposed to stay in the home. At the same time, Britain expanded the vote to more men in 1832, 1867 and 1884, which made it more obvious that women were left out because of their sex and not because of property.

At the start of the period, the main idea was that women were naturally inferior and should please men. Rousseau in Document 1 says woman is "made to please and to be in subjection to man," and that her "strength is in her charms." Rousseau was writing a book on education, so his purpose was to tell readers how girls should be raised, and this is important because he was not just describing women but trying to shape how they were trained to think. Wollstonecraft in Document 2 answers him directly, saying she wants women to have power "not over men; but over themselves." She argues that education and reason would make women better members of society. Her point is a big change in ideas, but it did not change laws right away.

By the middle of the 1800s, the arguments became more political. Mill in Document 3 says the "legal subordination of one sex to the other" is "wrong in itself" and should be replaced by "perfect equality." Mill had been a member of Parliament, and in 1867 he proposed an amendment to give women the vote, which was defeated. This shows that even a famous thinker inside Parliament could not change the law, and Mill himself admits in the document that opinions "rooted in the feelings" are hard to change by argument. Engels in Document 4 gives a different view, saying the oppression of women by men was the "first class oppression." Because Engels was a German socialist writing after Marx's death, his purpose was to connect women's problems to private property and class, so for him the vote alone would not free women. This shows that not everyone agreed on what women's liberation meant.

By the early 1900s, ideas turned into large organized movements. Fawcett in Document 6 says the National Union had 305 societies by 1911 and was "constantly and rapidly increasing." As president of the peaceful NUWSS, Fawcett wants to present her group as orderly and successful, and she even claims the movement had both "order" and "audacity," which may be a way to include the militants without endorsing them. Pankhurst in Document 7 disagrees, saying the old leaders were "content with expressions of sympathy" and that the WSPU motto was "Deeds, not words." Writing her autobiography in 1914, she wants to justify the militant tactics her group used. The poster in Document 5 shows uneven scales and says "Justice demands the vote," which was meant to persuade the public that women were treated unfairly.

Even with all this activity, the legal results were limited. Some laws did change, such as the British Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 that let married women keep their own property, and Finland gave women the vote in 1906. But Britain did not give women the vote until after the war, and in France the Napoleonic Code still kept wives under their husbands' authority. Overall, ideas and movements changed how people thought about women and created powerful campaigns, but by 1914 the law in most of Europe had only partly caught up.

Describes a broader development relevant to the prompt, such as Enlightenment debates on natural rights, the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Code, industrialization and the ideology of separate spheres, the expansion of the male franchise in the nineteenth century, or the growth of socialism and mass politics.

Uses document content to address the prompt: for example Rousseau's defense of female subjection, Wollstonecraft's and Mill's arguments for reason and equality, Engels's tie between women's oppression and class, and the suffrage poster, Fawcett, and Pankhurst as evidence of organized campaigning and its limits.

Uses specific evidence not found in the documents, such as the Napoleonic Code of 1804, the British Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882, the defeat of Mill's 1867 amendment, the Finnish grant of the vote to women in 1906, or suffragette hunger strikes and force-feeding.

Explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience matters for at least two documents, for example Fawcett's position as president of the peaceful NUWSS, Pankhurst's position as WSPU founder writing an autobiography in 1914, the persuasive aim of a poster made for a suffrage organization, or Engels writing as a German socialist in 1884.

Shows a complex understanding, for example by weighing intellectual change against limited legal change, by contrasting constitutional and militant strategies, by setting liberal feminism beside socialist analysis, or by comparing British outcomes with other European cases.

Evidence map (which documents support or complicate each line of reasoning):
- Enlightenment, liberal, and socialist ideas mounted a growing intellectual challenge to the assumption that women were naturally subordinate.. Supports: Document 2, 3, 4. Complicates: Document 1.
- Organized political movements turned arguments for equality into mass public campaigns that changed women's role in public life.. Supports: Document 5, 6, 7. Complicates: Document 3.
- The legal position of women, especially on the vote, changed only to a limited extent by 1914 because entrenched beliefs and politicians resisted reform.. Supports: Document 1, 3, 5, 7. Complicates: Document 6.
- Reformers disagreed about the causes of women's subordination and how to end it, which shaped and sometimes divided the movements.. Supports: Document 4, 6, 7. Complicates: Document 2.

Using the documents (use and sourcing):
- Document 1: Evidence of the eighteenth-century view that women were made to please men and be in subjection to them, which later reformers challenged and which helps explain how far change had to go. Sourcing: Rousseau wrote this in a 1762 book on education, so his claims about women are part of an educational program that rests on assumptions about nature. As a famous Enlightenment writer, his view carried influence, which is why later writers felt they had to answer it.
- Document 2: Shows an Enlightenment-based argument that women should be educated to use their own reason and have power over themselves, a direct challenge to Rousseau. Sourcing: Wollstonecraft published in 1792, during the French Revolution and its debates over rights. Because she was answering Rousseau directly, the excerpt shows ideas about women being argued over in print. Students should note that the quoted words are her rendering of Rousseau's argument.
- Document 3: States a liberal case that the legal subordination of women is wrong and should give way to perfect equality. It also concedes that opinions rooted in feeling resist argument, which helps explain why change was limited. Sourcing: Mill had been a member of Parliament from 1865 to 1868 and published the book in 1869, so he wrote with direct political experience at a time when the franchise was being debated. His standing as a well-known philosopher gave the argument a wide hearing.
- Document 4: Presents a socialist explanation that ties women's oppression to private property and class, suggesting that legal reform alone would not end it. Sourcing: Engels was a German socialist who published this in 1884, the year after Marx died, and he cites a manuscript he wrote with Marx. His purpose is to fit the family into a Marxist account of history, which shapes his emphasis on class over legal rights.
- Document 5: Shows that by 1909 organized suffragists were making a mass visual appeal that framed the vote as a matter of justice, with the uneven scales suggesting unequal treatment. It is also evidence that women still lacked the vote. Sourcing: Mary Lowndes designed the poster for a British women's suffrage organization, so it was made to persuade the public and is advocacy, not neutral description. The 1909 date places it during the most intense phase of the British campaign.
- Document 6: Shows the rapid growth of organized constitutional suffrage societies, which numbered 305 by October 1911, and claims that the movement combined order with audacity. Sourcing: As president of the NUWSS, which used peaceful methods, Fawcett had reason to stress her organization's size and success. Writing in 1912, before the vote was won, she also had reason to present the movement as respectable and growing.
- Document 7: Shows the founding of a women-only, militant organization with the motto Deeds, not words, and its frustration with older leaders and with politicians. This is evidence of division within the movement and of limited legislative results. Sourcing: Pankhurst founded the WSPU in 1903 and published this autobiography in 1914, so she was justifying her own militant strategy. That purpose explains her dismissive picture of the older constitutional leaders and of hypocritical politicians.

As president of the peaceful NUWSS, Fawcett wants to present her group as orderly and successful, and she even claims the movement had both "order" and "audacity," which may be a way to include the militants without endorsing them. Pankhurst in Document 7 disagrees, saying the old leaders were "content with expressions of sympathy" and that the WSPU motto was "Deeds, not words." Writing her autobiography in 1914, she wants to justify the militant tactics her group used. The poster in Document 5 shows uneven scales and says "Justice demands the vote," which was meant to persuade the public that women were treated unfairly.

Some laws did change, such as the British Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 that let married women keep their own property, and Finland gave women the vote in 1906. But Britain did not give women the vote until after the war, and in France the Napoleonic Code still kept wives under their husbands' authority. Overall, ideas and movements changed how people thought about women and created powerful campaigns, but by 1914 the law in most of Europe had only partly caught up.

Writers challenged old ideas and women built large campaigns, yet by 1914 women still could not vote in most European countries, so I think the change was moderate rather than total.

The documents show the change in ideas. Rousseau in 1762 says that woman is made to please man and to be in subjection to him, and that her strength is in her charms. This shows the view that women had to argue against. Mary Wollstonecraft answers him in 1792 by saying that she does not want women to have power over men but over themselves, and she wants women to use their own reason. So within about thirty years there was a direct challenge to the idea of subjection. Later, Pankhurst describes founding the Women's Social and Political Union, which was limited to women, free of party ties, and used the motto "Deeds, not words." This shows that by the early twentieth century women were organizing their own political movement and not just writing books.

Wollstonecraft's purpose matters for how we use her. She was writing to answer Rousseau and to persuade educated readers that women's education needed to change, so her book is an argument and not proof that anything had changed yet. Pankhurst's point of view also matters. She wrote her autobiography in 1914 as the founder of the WSPU, so she wants to make her group look bold and to make the older leaders look weak when she says they were content with sympathy from hypocritical politicians. defensible_theses: Between 1762 and 1914, writers such as Wollstonecraft and Mill turned the assumption of natural female subjection into a contested political question, and later movements turned that argument into mass organizing; even so, the legal change that followed was partial. By 1914 married women in Britain had gained property rights, but most European women still had no national vote.

Organized political movements did more than abstract ideas to change women's position. The NUWSS network of more than 300 societies and the militant WSPU made women's rights a public issue that governments could not ignore, though their arguments over tactics also show how hard it was to win the parliamentary vote.

Ideas and movements changed women's social and educational position more than their legal standing. Liberal and socialist critiques reached wide audiences and women entered public campaigning, but as Mill predicted, ideas about women rooted in feeling outlasted the arguments against them. Rousseau's model of separate roles survived in law codes and political practice until 1914.
contextualization_ideas: Enlightenment natural rights thought and the French Revolution raised claims of universal rights. Olympe de Gouges and Wollstonecraft applied those claims to women, but the revolutionaries closed women's political clubs in 1793 and the Napoleonic Code of 1804 placed wives under their husbands' authority.

Industrialization and the growth of the middle class strengthened the ideology of separate spheres, which assigned women to the home. At the same time, women's factory work led to protective laws such as the Mines Act of 1842.

Over the nineteenth century the male franchise expanded through the Reform Acts of 1832, 1867, and 1884, and mass politics and socialism grew. Women's exclusion from the vote therefore became more visible and more organized movements formed to challenge it.
outside_evidence: Olympe de Gouges published the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen in 1791 and was executed in 1793.
In 1793 the French revolutionary government banned women's political clubs.
The Napoleonic Code of 1804 required a wife to obey her husband and limited married women's control of property.
The Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857 created civil divorce courts in England.
In 1867 Mill proposed an amendment to the Second Reform Bill replacing the word man with person, and the House of Commons defeated it.
The Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 let married women in Britain keep their own earnings and property.
Josephine Butler led the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts, which were repealed in 1886.
Girton College, Cambridge, was founded for women in 1869.

August Bebel's Woman and Socialism, published in 1879, linked women's emancipation to socialist revolution. In 1910 Clara Zetkin proposed an International Women's Day at a socialist women's conference in Copenhagen.
Finland gave women the national vote in 1906 and Norway did so in 1913.
Imprisoned suffragettes went on hunger strike and were force-fed from 1909, and the Cat and Mouse Act of 1913 allowed hunger strikers to be released and then rearrested.
Emily Wilding Davison died after running onto the course at the 1913 Derby.

evidence_map.line: Enlightenment, liberal, and socialist ideas mounted a growing intellectual challenge to the assumption that women were naturally subordinate.
Organized political movements turned arguments for equality into mass public campaigns that changed women's role in public life.
The legal position of women, especially on the vote, changed only to a limited extent by 1914 because entrenched beliefs and politicians resisted reform.
Reformers disagreed about the causes of women's subordination and how to end it, which shaped and sometimes divided the movements.

samples.essay:
Between 1762 and 1914, ideas about women's equality changed a great deal, but the legal position of women changed much less. Writers like Wollstonecraft and Mill attacked the idea that women were naturally meant to obey men, and by the late 1800s these arguments had turned into organized mass movements. However, the movements were divided over methods, and by 1914 most European women still could not vote in national elections, so the change was mostly in ideas and organization and only partly in law.

The debate over women took place in a wider context of Enlightenment arguments about natural rights and reason. Thinkers argued that all men had rights by nature, and the French Revolution put these ideas into practice for men, but not for women. Later, industrialization helped spread the ideology of separate spheres, where middle class men worked in public and women were supposed to stay in the home. At the same time, Britain expanded the vote to more men in 1832, 1867 and 1884, which made it more obvious that women were left out because of their sex and not because of property.

At the start of the period, the main idea was that women were naturally inferior and should please men. Rousseau in Document 1 says woman is "made to please and to be in subjection to man," and that her "strength is in her charms." Rousseau was writing a book on education, so his purpose was to tell readers how girls should be raised, and this is important because he was not just describing women but trying to shape how they were trained to think. Wollstonecraft in Document 2 answers him directly, saying she wants women to have power "not over men; but over themselves." She argues that education and reason would make women better members of society. Her point is a big change in ideas, but it did not change laws right away.

By the middle of the 1800s, the arguments became more political. Mill in Document 3 says the "legal subordination of one sex to the other" is "wrong in itself" and should be replaced by "perfect equality." Mill had been a member of Parliament, and in 1867 he proposed an amendment to give women the vote, which was defeated. This shows that even a famous thinker inside Parliament could not change the law, and Mill himself admits in the document that opinions "rooted in the feelings" are hard to change by argument. Engels in Document 4 gives a different view, saying the oppression of women by men was the "first class oppression." Because Engels was a German socialist writing after Marx's death, his purpose was to connect women's problems to private property and class, so for him the vote alone would not free women. This shows that not everyone agreed on what women's liberation meant.

By the early 1900s, ideas turned into large organized movements. Fawcett in Document 6 says the National Union had 305 societies by 1911 and was "constantly and rapidly increasing." As president of the peaceful NUWSS, Fawcett wants to present her group as orderly and successful, and she even claims the movement had both "order" and "audacity," which may be a way to include the militants without endorsing them. Pankhurst in Document 7 disagrees, saying the old leaders were "content with expressions of sympathy" and that the WSPU motto was "Deeds, not words." Writing her autobiography in 1914, she wants to justify the militant tactics her group used. The poster in Document 5 shows uneven scales and says "Justice demands the vote," which was meant to persuade the public that women were treated unfairly.

parts.prompt:
Between the fifteenth and the late eighteenth centuries, Europe went from a Latin Christendom under a single church to a continent split among Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and other confessions. In the same centuries, monarchs and other governments claimed more and more power over religion, and some of them later turned to policies of limited toleration.

Evaluate the extent to which religious change and religious conflict transformed the relationship between religious authority and political authority in Europe from c. 1450 to c. 1789. You are not expected to address the entire time period.

In your response you should do the following:
- Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
- Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
- Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least two pieces of specific and relevant evidence.
- Use historical reasoning (causation, comparison, or continuity and change) to frame or structure an argument that addresses the prompt.
- Use evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the prompt, demonstrating a complex understanding.
parts.model_answer:
Between 1450 and 1789, religious change and conflict greatly transformed the relationship between religious and political authority, because power over the church moved away from the pope and toward kings and princes. However, this transformation was not complete. Rulers took control of churches, but for most of the period they still believed that one shared religion was needed to keep a state stable, and real toleration only came slowly, usually for practical reasons rather than out of principle. The Reformation broke the pope's authority, the wars of religion forced rulers to make settlements, and later the Enlightenment pushed some monarchs toward limited toleration.

Even before Luther, the authority of the papacy was weakening. During the Avignon papacy and the Great Schism, there were at times two or even three men claiming to be pope, which made many people question the church's leadership. Thinkers like Jan Hus in Bohemia criticized church corruption, and the conciliar movement argued that church councils should have authority over the pope. At the same time, monarchs in places like France and Spain were building stronger territorial states and wanted more control over church appointments and money. The printing press also let new religious ideas spread quickly. All of this meant that when Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses in 1517, there were rulers ready to use religious reform to increase their own power.

The clearest change was that political rulers began to take over religious authority directly. In England, Henry VIII wanted an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, and when the pope would not give it, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in 1534, making the king the head of the Church of England. This shows that the king, not Rome, now had final authority over religion in England. In the Holy Roman Empire, the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 allowed each prince to choose whether his territory would be Lutheran or Catholic, which is the idea of "cuius regio, eius religio." This settlement put religious choice in the hands of political rulers, and it showed that conflict between Catholics and Lutherans had made it impossible for the emperor or the pope to force one faith on everyone.

However, these changes did not mean the end of the idea that a state needed one religion. Augsburg did not give toleration to individuals, and it left out Calvinists completely, which helped lead to the Thirty Years' War. Catholic states also show continuity. The kings of France and Spain gained a lot of control over their churches without ever breaking with Rome, so increasing state power over religion was not only a Protestant development. In France, Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, giving Huguenots limited rights to worship, but this was a compromise to end the wars of religion, not a belief in toleration. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685 because he believed in "one king, one law, one faith," and many Huguenots fled the country. This shows that the old belief in religious unity was still strong more than a century after the Reformation started.

Change did continue later in the period. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 recognized Calvinism and largely ended the era of major religious wars, and after this, religion became less of a reason for wars between states. In the eighteenth century, Enlightenment writers like Voltaire attacked religious persecution, and Joseph II of Austria issued a Patent of Toleration in 1781 that gave Protestants and Orthodox Christians more rights. Still, even this toleration was granted from above by a ruler who kept control over the church, so it actually shows how much power the state now had over religion.

Overall, religious change and conflict transformed the relationship by shifting authority over the church from the pope to the state, but the belief that religion was tied to political order lasted for most of the period, and toleration was limited and controlled by rulers.

rows.task_specific: Continuity and change (or causation or comparison) used to frame the argument, for example change from papal supremacy to state-controlled churches alongside continuity in the belief that religious unity guaranteed political order. Complex understanding might come from tracing both change and continuity across regions, comparing Protestant and Catholic states, explaining several causes, or qualifying the argument with counterevidence such as Catholic monarchs who gained church control without breaking with Rome.

scoring_notes: Responses may concentrate on c. 1450 to c. 1648 or move into the eighteenth century. Full coverage of the span is not required, but the argument must address the extent of change.
Evidence may come from any part of Europe, including Poland-Lithuania, the Habsburg lands, Scandinavia, Iberia, and the British Isles.
A narrative of Reformation events without a judgment about how church-state relations changed should not earn the analysis points.
The complexity point is earned through sustained argument, not a single sentence that mentions another perspective.

defensible_theses: Religious conflict deeply changed the relationship between church and state: rulers in Protestant and Catholic lands alike took control of religious institutions. Yet until the late eighteenth century most governments still assumed that religious uniformity was necessary for political stability.

The Reformation and the religious wars moved authority over religion from the papacy to territorial rulers, as the Peace of Augsburg and the Peace of Westphalia show. After 1648, exhaustion from war and Enlightenment ideas pushed some states toward limited toleration. That toleration was granted by the state, not won as a right.

The change was more limited than it first appears. Many Catholic monarchs, such as Francis I through the Concordat of Bologna, had already gained great control over the church before the Reformation. Confessional persecution continued long after 1648, as Louis XIV's revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 shows.
contextualization_ideas: Late medieval challenges to papal authority, including the Avignon papacy, the Great Schism, the conciliar movement, and the reform movements of John Wycliffe and Jan Hus, had already weakened papal prestige before 1517.
The printing press and Christian humanism, such as Erasmus's work on the Greek New Testament, spread criticism of clerical abuses and made religious debate available to a wider public.
The growth of New Monarchies in France, England, and Spain, and the fragmented political structure of the Holy Roman Empire, shaped how rulers could use religious change to increase their own power.
outside_evidence: Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses (1517) and his appearance at the Diet of Worms (1521) depended on protection from Frederick the Wise of Saxony, which showed how princes could shelter religious reform.
Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy (1534) made the English monarch head of the Church of England, and the dissolution of the monasteries (1536 to 1541) moved church wealth to the crown.
The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let each prince of the Holy Roman Empire choose between Lutheranism and Catholicism for his territory, a principle later summarized as cuius regio, eius religio.

The French Wars of Religion, including the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572), ended with Henry IV's Edict of Nantes (1598), which granted Huguenots limited toleration. Louis XIV revoked it with the Edict of Fontainebleau (1685).
The Dutch Revolt against Philip II of Spain combined religious grievances with political ones. It led to the Union of Utrecht (1579) and the Act of Abjuration (1581).
The Council of Trent (1545 to 1563) and the Jesuit order (approved in 1540) strengthened Catholic doctrine and education, often in alliance with Catholic rulers such as the Habsburgs.

The Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) began with the Defenestration of Prague. Cardinal Richelieu's Catholic France supported Protestant Sweden against the Habsburgs. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) recognized Calvinism and confirmed the princes' authority over religion in their territories.
The Warsaw Confederation (1573) in Poland-Lithuania guaranteed religious peace among the nobility.
The Spanish Inquisition (established in 1478) and the expulsion of Jews from Spain (1492) show monarchs enforcing religious unity as a policy of state.

The Glorious Revolution (1688 to 1689) and the Toleration Act (1689) gave Protestant Dissenters in England freedom of worship but kept Catholics and Dissenters out of full political rights. John Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration (1689) argued for separating religious belief from civil government.

Voltaire campaigned over the Calas affair (1762) and wrote the Treatise on Tolerance (1763). Joseph II's Patent of Toleration (1781) and France's Edict of Versailles (1787) reflected Enlightenment-era toleration granted by the state.
Portugal (1759), France (1764), and Spain (1767) expelled the Jesuits, and Pope Clement XIV suppressed the order in 1773. This shows Catholic monarchs placing the church under state interests.
common_pitfalls: Writing a narrative of the Reformation without judging how far relations between church and state changed.
Assuming that religious toleration began in 1648, or ignoring persecution after Westphalia, such as the revocation of the Edict of Nantes.
Treating only Protestant states as gaining control over churches, while ignoring Catholic examples such as the Concordat of Bologna or the expulsions of the Jesuits.
Mixing up the Peace of Augsburg, which covered only Lutherans and Catholics, with the Peace of Westphalia, which added Calvinists.
Reducing every religious war to a single cause instead of recognizing that dynastic, political, and religious motives were combined.
Moving into United States history, such as the First Amendment, instead of keeping the focus on Europe.

The English Act of Supremacy was passed in 1534.

samples.essay:
Between 1450 and 1789, religious change and conflict greatly transformed the relationship between religious and political authority, because power over the church moved away from the pope and toward kings and princes. However, this transformation was not complete. Rulers took control of churches, but for most of the period they still believed that one shared religion was needed to keep a state stable, and real toleration only came slowly, usually for practical reasons rather than out of principle. The Reformation broke the pope's authority, the wars of religion forced rulers to make settlements, and later the Enlightenment pushed some monarchs toward limited toleration.

Even before Luther, the authority of the papacy was weakening. During the Avignon papacy and the Great Schism, there were at times two or even three men claiming to be pope, which made many people question the church's leadership. Thinkers like Jan Hus in Bohemia criticized church corruption, and the conciliar movement argued that church councils should have authority over the pope. At the same time, monarchs in places like France and Spain were building stronger territorial states and wanted more control over church appointments and money. The printing press also let new religious ideas spread quickly. All of this meant that when Luther posted his Ninety-Five Theses in 1517, there were rulers ready to use religious reform to increase their own power.

The clearest change was that political rulers began to take over religious authority directly. In England, Henry VIII wanted an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, and when the pope would not give it, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in 1534, making the king the head of the Church of England. This shows that the king, not Rome, now had final authority over religion in England. In the Holy Roman Empire, the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 allowed each prince to choose whether his territory would be Lutheran or Catholic, which is the idea of "cuius regio, eius religio." This settlement put religious choice in the hands of political rulers, and it showed that conflict between Catholics and Lutherans had made it impossible for the emperor or the pope to force one faith on everyone.

However, these changes did not mean the end of the idea that a state needed one religion. Augsburg did not give toleration to individuals, and it left out Calvinists completely, which helped lead to the Thirty Years' War. Catholic states also show continuity. The kings of France and Spain gained a lot of control over their churches without ever breaking with Rome, so increasing state power over religion was not only a Protestant development. In France, Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, giving Huguenots limited rights to worship, but this was a compromise to end the wars of religion, not a belief in toleration. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685 because he believed in "one king, one law, one faith," and many Huguenots fled the country. This shows that the old belief in religious unity was still strong more than a century after the Reformation started.

Change did continue later in the period. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 recognized Calvinism and largely ended the era of major religious wars, and after this, religion became less of a reason for wars between states. In the eighteenth century, Enlightenment writers like Voltaire attacked religious persecution, and Joseph II of Austria issued a Patent of Toleration in 1781 that gave Protestants and Orthodox Christians more rights. Still, even this toleration was granted from above by a ruler who kept control over the church, so it actually shows how much power the state now had over religion.

Overall, religious change and conflict transformed the relationship by shifting authority over the church from the pope to the state, but the belief that religion was tied to political order lasted for most of the period, and toleration was limited and controlled by rulers.

samples.essay:
Religious change and religious conflict changed the relationship between religious authority and political authority in Europe a great deal between 1450 and 1789, because the Pope lost power over rulers in many places and governments gained more control over religion. However, rulers still wanted religion to support their rule, so the change was not total. This essay will look at England and the Holy Roman Empire.

In England the biggest change came under Henry VIII. Henry wanted a divorce from Catherine of Aragon, and the Pope would not give it to him. In 1534 Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, which made the king the head of the Church of England. After this the English church was no longer under the Pope. Henry also closed the monasteries and took their land. Later rulers like Mary and Elizabeth changed the religion back and forth, which shows that the monarch was now the one deciding what the church believed. This shows that political authority took over a lot of religious authority in England.

In the Holy Roman Empire, Martin Luther started the Reformation in 1517 when he criticized the Catholic Church, and many German princes became Lutheran. There were wars between Catholic and Lutheran princes. In 1555 the Peace of Augsburg was signed. It said that each prince could choose whether his territory would be Catholic or Lutheran. This meant that the princes, not the Pope or the emperor, decided the religion of the people who lived under them. Later, the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War and added Calvinism to the options. Subjects still had to follow the religion of their ruler in most cases.

These examples show that religion and politics were linked in new ways. In England the king became head of the church, and in Germany the princes picked the religion. Both of these took power away from the Pope. At the same time, the rulers still did not allow much freedom, so people who did not follow the official church could still be treated badly. Some things did stay the same because the ruler still used religion to keep control of his people.

In conclusion, religious change and conflict changed church and state relations a lot because the Pope lost authority and rulers gained it, as seen in England and the Holy Roman Empire, but some continuity remained because rulers kept using religion for political purposes.

samples.essay:
Religious change and religious conflict changed the relationship between religious authority and political authority a lot in Europe from 1450 to 1789. Rulers became more powerful and the church became less powerful, though some things stayed the same.

Before the Reformation, the Catholic Church had a lot of power in Europe. But in the late Middle Ages the church was already being challenged. The popes were weakened by the Avignon papacy and then the Great Schism, when there were rival popes, and people like Wycliffe and Hus criticized the church. Kings in places like France and England were also building stronger territorial states, and they did not want the pope to have so much influence over their lands. The printing press later helped spread new ideas. This background made it easier for the Reformation to challenge the authority of the church, and it shows that the balance between religion and politics was already shifting before Martin Luther.

When the Reformation came, many rulers took control of religion in their lands. In England, Henry VIII broke with Rome and made himself head of the church. This shows how political authority grew over religious authority. Other rulers did similar things in their own states.

There were many wars over religion, and these wars were very destructive. Over time, some governments started to be more tolerant, so the relationship kept changing. In conclusion, religion and politics were changed by the Reformation, because kings gained more power and the church lost some of its power.
